title: As to a friend
hook: Kristin Neff's research on self-compassion: kindness to yourself, shared humanity, mindfulness
carry: what would I say to a friend

segments.voice: Yesterday: karuna, the wish that others be free from suffering. Your line: silently wish them well. Today the wish turns around.

Your friend calls. She forgot an important meeting, her boss was annoyed, and she feels like an idiot. What do you say? Probably: that's awful, but it happens to everyone, you're not an idiot, what do you need? Now you forgot the meeting. Listen to what Brewer calls the chatter. Idiot. Always like this. Everyone saw. Said to a friend, those words would end the friendship. In the early 2000s a psychologist named Kristin Neff started studying what happens when people take the voice they use for a friend and point it inward.
screen: `YOUR FRIEND FORGOT THE MEETING.` → `NOW YOU FORGOT IT.` → `YOU'D NEVER TALK TO HER LIKE THAT.`

segments.voice: Neff described self-compassion in three parts, each set against its opposite. First, kindness to yourself instead of harsh judgment: not pretending the mistake didn't happen, but talking to yourself about it the way a good friend would. Second, shared humanity instead of isolation. Failing can feel like you're the only one. The room is full: other people forget meetings, lose their temper, lie awake at 2am. Third, mindfulness instead of getting swept away. You see the pain clearly, without shoving it down and without making it the whole story. Now the obvious objection: if I'm kind to myself, won't I stop trying? The research points the other way. In one set of studies at Berkeley, people nudged toward self-compassion after a failure studied longer for a retest, and were more willing to make amends for a past wrong, than people nudged toward self-esteem. Kindness seems to make it safer to look at what went wrong. A caution: much of this research is correlation and short experiments. Encouraging, not a miracle. The idea is also old. In the Pali texts, King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika admit to each other that no one is dearer to them than themselves. The Buddha doesn't scold them. He says that searching in every direction you find no one dearer than yourself, and since everyone feels this way, whoever cares for themselves should not harm another. Self-regard, in that telling, is where regard for others starts.
screen: `KINDNESS, NOT HARSH JUDGMENT.` · `SHARED HUMANITY, NOT ISOLATION.` · `MINDFULNESS, NOT GETTING SWEPT AWAY.` · `KINDNESS MAKES IT SAFER TO LOOK.` · then, large: `AS TO A FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've been hard on yourself about lately, hear what your inner voice says about it, then imagine a friend telling you that exact story about themselves. Silently say to yourself what you'd say back to them, even if it feels awkward. Then add one line: other people have done this too.
Neff, who named self-compassion's three parts, kindness, shared humanity and mindfulness: the voice you'd use for a friend, turned inward.
Your line: what would I say to a friend. The kind voice was yours all along. Day three hundred fourteen, done.

howItsDone: In self-compassion practice, developed from Kristin Neff's research, people notice their pain, remind themselves others go through the same, and speak to themselves as they would to a friend.

chat.says: If I'm kind to myself after a mistake, won't I just stop trying?
options: Studies point the other way: kindness made people study longer and make amends.
Yes. Harsh self-talk is what keeps people improving after they fail.
No, because self-compassion means acting as if the mistake never happened.
